cls: Drug class overview - prokinetic agents (gastrointestinal motility stimulants)
pharm: Class of drugs that enhance gastrointestinal motility and accelerate gastric emptying/transit, used for gastroparesis, functional dyspepsia, gastro-oesophageal reflux, and nausea/vomiting; 'plain' denotes single-agent prokinetics (not combinations).
quick: Agent-specific (e.g., metoclopramide 10 mg up to TID short-term; domperidone 10 mg up to TID; itopride 50 mg TID; prucalopride 2 mg once daily) - refer to the individual drug
Most prokinetics are taken 15-30 minutes before meals (and at bedtime where relevant)
Agent-specific; metoclopramide is often used short-term, others vary - check the individual drug
Several (e.g., metoclopramide, prucalopride) need renal dose reduction - check the individual drug
Agent-specific dose considerations - check the individual drug
Avoid - additive sedation with centrally acting agents (e.g., metoclopramide)
Extrapyramidal/neurological effects, QT interval (some agents), symptom response
summary: Gastroprokinetics (prokinetic agents) are a class of drugs that stimulate and coordinate gastrointestinal smooth-muscle activity to accelerate gastric emptying and gut transit. 'Plain' indicates single-agent prokinetics rather than fixed-dose combinations. The class includes dopamine D2 antagonists (metoclopramide, domperidone), the dual D2-antagonist/acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor itopride, 5-HT4 receptor agonists (prucalopride; historically cisapride, now restricted, and mosapride), and motilin-receptor agonists (e.g., erythromycin used off-label). They are used for diabetic and idiopathic gastroparesis, functional dyspepsia, gastro-oesophageal reflux, and prevention/treatment of nausea and vomiting. Because effects, dosing, contraindications, and warnings differ markedly between agents, this is a CLASS OVERVIEW: prescribe and dose the specific drug. Key class-wide cautions are extrapyramidal/neurological effects (D2 antagonists, especially metoclopramide), QT prolongation/cardiac arrhythmia (domperidone, cisapride), and avoidance in GI obstruction, perforation, or haemorrhage.
indications: Gastroparesis (diabetic or idiopathic delayed gastric emptying)
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease as an adjunct (selected agents)

dosage.d: 10 mg up to three times daily before meals; limit to <=5 days to reduce tardive dyskinesia risk; reduce dose in renal impairment
dosage.n: Max recommended duration 5 days; avoid long-term use

dosage.d: 10 mg up to three times daily before meals; lowest effective dose for shortest time (QT risk)
dosage.n: Avoid in cardiac conduction/QT risk; restricted by some regulators

dosage.d: 50 mg three times daily before meals
2 mg once daily (1 mg in significant renal impairment or elderly)
Low-dose (e.g., 3 mg/kg IV or 50-250 mg orally) before meals for gastroparesis
dosage.n: Tachyphylaxis with prolonged use; QT and interaction risks

admin: Identify and use the specific prokinetic agent - dosing and warnings are agent-specific
Most oral prokinetics are taken 15-30 minutes before meals (and at bedtime if directed)
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary duration, especially metoclopramide (extrapyramidal risk) and domperidone (cardiac risk)
Exclude mechanical GI obstruction, perforation, or haemorrhage before use
Adjust dose for renal/hepatic function and review concomitant QT-prolonging or interacting drugs per the individual agent
moa: Prokinetics enhance gastrointestinal motility through several mechanisms depending on the agent. Dopamine D2-receptor antagonists (metoclopramide, domperidone, itopride) block inhibitory dopaminergic tone in the GI tract, increasing lower-oesophageal sphincter tone, gastric contractility, and antroduodenal coordination, and also act on the chemoreceptor trigger zone to produce an antiemetic effect (metoclopramide additionally has 5-HT4 agonist and, at high doses, 5-HT3 antagonist activity; itopride also inhibits acetylcholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine). Selective 5-HT4 receptor agonists (prucalopride, mosapride) stimulate enteric cholinergic neurons to promote peristalsis. Motilin-receptor agonists (erythromycin) trigger migrating motor complexes to accelerate gastric emptying.

absolute: Gastrointestinal mechanical obstruction, perforation, or haemorrhage (prokinetic stimulation is hazardous)
Known hypersensitivity to the specific agent
relative: Parkinson disease and other movement disorders (D2 antagonists may worsen)
Cardiac conduction disorders, QT prolongation, significant electrolyte disturbance (domperidone, cisapride)
Concomitant strong CYP3A4 inhibitors with domperidone (QT risk)
monitor: Extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia (D2 antagonists)
QT interval and cardiac rhythm (domperidone; cisapride)
Symptom response and need for continued therapy
Renal/hepatic function as relevant to the chosen agent

preg: Pregnancy use is agent-specific. Metoclopramide has extensive data and is often used short-term for nausea/vomiting in pregnancy; domperidone and newer agents have more limited data. Always consult the individual drug's prescribing information and use the agent best supported for the indication.
lact: Lactation considerations differ by agent. Metoclopramide and domperidone pass into milk in small amounts (domperidone has even been used off-label to promote lactation, though cardiac safety concerns exist); refer to the specific drug's information before use while breastfeeding.
renal: Several prokinetics require renal dose adjustment - for example, reduce metoclopramide in significant renal impairment, and reduce prucalopride to 1 mg once daily in severe renal impairment. Check the individual agent and adjust accordingly.
hepatic: Hepatic dose considerations are agent-specific. Domperidone is contraindicated in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment; other agents may need caution. Refer to the chosen drug's prescribing information.

major: Domperidone with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (azole antifungals, macrolides, protease inhibitors) or other QT-prolonging drugs - increased risk of serious arrhythmia
D2 antagonists with antipsychotics or other dopamine antagonists - additive extrapyramidal effects
Metoclopramide with MAO inhibitors and other serotonergic drugs - risk of serotonin syndrome/hypertension
moderate: Prokinetics alter the rate of gastric emptying and thus the absorption of many co-administered drugs
Anticholinergics and opioids antagonise prokinetic effects
CNS depressants/alcohol - additive sedation with centrally acting agents (metoclopramide)
minor: 5-HT4 agonists generally have fewer drug interactions but check individual profiles
interactions.food: Most prokinetics are taken before meals to optimise their effect on gastric emptying.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol with centrally acting agents (e.g., metoclopramide) due to additive sedation.
interactions.diagnostics: Some agents (domperidone, cisapride) require baseline ECG/electrolyte assessment in at-risk patients; metoclopramide can transiently raise prolactin.

common: Diarrhoea or abdominal cramping (5-HT4 agonists, erythromycin)
Hyperprolactinaemia effects (galactorrhoea, menstrual changes) with D2 antagonists
serious: Extrapyramidal reactions, acute dystonia, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia (metoclopramide, other D2 antagonists)
QT prolongation and serious ventricular arrhythmia (domperidone; cisapride)

monitoring: Neurological status for extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia (D2 antagonists)
ECG/QT interval and electrolytes for domperidone and other QT-affecting agents in at-risk patients
Symptom response (gastric emptying, nausea, bowel function) and duration of therapy
Renal/hepatic function relevant to the specific agent
counsel: These medicines help your stomach empty and move food along; take them as directed, usually before meals
Use them only for as long as advised - some (like metoclopramide) can cause movement disorders if used too long or at high doses
Report uncontrolled movements, muscle stiffness, restlessness, or a fast/irregular heartbeat straight away
Avoid alcohol with sedating prokinetics; tell your doctor about all your other medicines and any heart rhythm problems
This is a group of different drugs - follow the specific instructions for the exact medicine you have been prescribed
pk: Oral prokinetic effect generally within 30-60 minutes; IV metoclopramide/erythromycin within minutes
Plasma peaks typically within 1-3 hours for oral agents (agent-specific)
Agent-specific (e.g., metoclopramide ~5-6 h; domperidone ~7-9 h; prucalopride ~24 h)
Dosing frequency reflects half-life - several agents are given before each main meal
Store each product per its own label, generally at room temperature protected from light and moisture
pearls: GROUP/CLASS ENTRY - 'Gastroprokinetics Plain' is not a single drug but the class of single-agent prokinetics; identify and dose the specific drug (metoclopramide, domperidone, itopride, prucalopride, erythromycin, etc.)

Class-wide safety flags: extrapyramidal/tardive dyskinesia with metoclopramide (limit to <=5 days), QT prolongation/arrhythmia with domperidone and cisapride, and avoidance in GI obstruction/perforation/haemorrhage
Cisapride has been withdrawn or severely restricted in many countries due to fatal arrhythmias; domperidone now carries cardiac restrictions and dose/duration limits
Most prokinetics are dosed before meals; use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration
Because dosing and warnings differ greatly, always consult the individual agent's official label/SmPC rather than a generic class dose
missed: Dosing schedules differ by agent; in general, take a missed dose before your next meal if remembered in time, otherwise skip it and resume the usual schedule - do not double up. Follow the specific instructions for the exact prokinetic prescribed.
overdose: Overdose features are agent-specific. D2 antagonists (metoclopramide) can cause drowsiness, confusion, and extrapyramidal reactions (treat dystonia with anticholinergics such as procyclidine/benztropine; antihistamines may help). Domperidone and cisapride overdose can cause serious arrhythmias - monitor ECG and electrolytes. There is generally no specific antidote; provide supportive care, manage cardiac and neurological effects, and consult the individual product information and poisons resources.
